SSRN preprint, March 2026 (preliminary version) · DOI [10.2139/ssrn.7013178](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7013178) · earlier, broader version of [*Characteristic-Space Metrics*](/research/characteristic-space-metrics.qmd) · grows out of the PhD thesis (listed on SSRN under Yang Liu)
:::

::: {.standfirst}
Investors describe each stock by dozens of traits, many of them near-copies of one another. Before a model can say which combinations of traits earn a risk premium, it must decide when two combinations are genuinely different. The paper takes the ruler for that decision from the data and rebuilds instrumented principal component analysis (IPCA) on it. In simulations calibrated to U.S. stocks, with the true priced directions placed by design on the combinations along which characteristics vary most, the rebuilt estimator (NA-IPCA) recovers them. On a distance scale from 0 (exact recovery) to about 1.73 (the largest possible distance for three directions), it scores 0.01 and an IPCA benchmark with no intercept block (no room for expected return that no factor explains) scores 0.73 <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Table 8, p. 38">(Table 8, p. 38)</span>.
:::

## The question {#gf-question}

In the agenda, this paper asks the first question: which ruler? The next paper, [*Characteristic-Space Metrics*](/research/characteristic-space-metrics.qmd), asks: once the ruler is chosen, what does it decide, and how precisely?

**Firm characteristics overlap and differ in spread. Which combinations of them are genuinely distinct sources of priced risk, and which are only near-copies or leftovers?**

To say how much of a stock's expected return each driver explains, a model must first decide when two combinations of characteristics are really different, and how large each one is. The rule it uses for that is the ruler. Give each characteristic a weight and add them up: every stock gets a score. Such a weighted combination is called a direction (it is not a portfolio). The plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric) judges a direction by its weights alone. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) judges it by the scores it gives real stocks: how large they typically are, and whether two directions' scores line up across stocks, high on the same stocks and low on the same stocks.

The ruler, then, is the convention a model uses to measure how large a direction is and how much two directions overlap. Two value signals that pick out the same cheap stocks count as overlapping under the characteristic ruler but as unrelated under the plain ruler. Standard methods such as principal component analysis (PCA), IPCA [@kelly2019characteristics] and many machine-learning estimators use the plain ruler <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 1.1, p. 2">(Section 1.1, p. 2)</span>. IPCA is a standard method in which characteristics decide how strongly each stock moves with the common drivers. The paper's abstract calls the characteristic ruler "a hidden ruler" <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: abstract, p. 1">(p. 1)</span>.

The model has three blocks: hidden factors inferred from the data, observed factors such as the market, and the intercept: the part of expected return that no factor in this model explains (the home page's "alpha" is a close relative, measured against a stated benchmark model).

**The answer in one sentence.** Measure combinations with the characteristic ruler, taken from how characteristics spread and overlap across stocks; in simulations calibrated to U.S. stocks, where the true priced directions are placed by design on the combinations along which characteristics vary most, the estimator built on this ruler (NA-IPCA) recovers them and an IPCA benchmark with no intercept block does not.

## Why it matters {#gf-why}

The ruler decides what counts as "different". Under the plain ruler, two directions can look unrelated and still pick out the same stocks, so a model can split one priced direction into two factors, let a hidden factor copy an observed benchmark factor already in the model, or push priced content into the intercept <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 1.1, pp. 2–3">(Section 1.1, pp. 2–3)</span>.

- **Practical.** The paper argues that its ruler stops hidden factors from merely reproducing benchmark portfolios, giving users such as portfolio managers a sharper line between priced structure, benchmark exposure and residual noise <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Sections 1.4–1.5, pp. 5–6">(Sections 1.4–1.5, pp. 5–6)</span>. This is argued and simulated, not shown on live portfolios.
- **Statistical.** A good fit does not reveal the right structure: in the paper's simulations IPCA fits returns best while missing the true directions <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 7.3, p. 40; Table 9, p. 42">(Table 9, p. 42)</span>.

## The argument at a glance {#gf-map}

::: {.logic-map}
1. **Question.** Stocks are described by dozens of characteristics, many of them versions of a few traits <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 6.2, p. 28">(Section 6.2, p. 28)</span>. → [The question](#gf-question)
2. **Why.** Because of this overlap, the plain ruler that PCA and IPCA use misjudges which combinations are truly different <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 1.1, p. 2">(Section 1.1, p. 2)</span>. → [Why it matters](#gf-why)
3. **Framework.** Estimate the characteristic ruler from the data and write all the model's rules in it, including how the three blocks are kept apart and how much the intercept may carry. The result is NA-IPCA. → [The framework](#gf-framework)
4. **Mechanism.** Directions that look unrelated under the plain ruler can overlap under the characteristic ruler, so separating the blocks with the characteristic ruler stops double counting. → [A simple example](#gf-example)
5. **Evidence.** The U.S. characteristic ruler is strongly uneven. In the headline simulation NA-IPCA recovers the priced directions and an IPCA benchmark with no intercept block misses them, a comparison that does not isolate the ruler. IPCA comes close in the paper's efficiency and stress-test designs and stays far off (0.73–0.99) in the metric and correlation sweeps <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Tables 9–10, pp. 42–43; Tables 16–19, pp. 62–64">(Tables 9–10, 16–19)</span>. → [Design and main results](#gf-results)
6. **Contribution.** The ruler becomes an explicit, estimated part of the model's economics; IPCA is the special case with the plain ruler and a non-binding cap on the intercept <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: p. 22">(p. 22)</span>. → [How it relates to prior work](#gf-literature)
7. **Boundary.** The paper does not test NA-IPCA on real returns or portfolios; a real-data application is left to a separate study <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 8, pp. 50–51">(pp. 50–51)</span>. → [Scope](#gf-scope)
:::

## The framework {#gf-framework}

Let $Z_t$ hold $L$ characteristics for the $N_t$ stocks observed in month $t$. The characteristic ruler is the long-run average of how characteristics spread and move together across stocks <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 2, p. 6">(Section 2, p. 6)</span>:

$$
Q_Z = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{N_t} Z_t^{\top} Z_t .
$$

Under this ruler, the size of a direction with weights $a$ is $(a^{\top} Q_Z a)^{1/2}$: roughly, how widely the scores it gives stocks vary. The plain ruler replaces $Q_Z$ with the identity matrix.

Expected excess returns are split into the three blocks <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 2, p. 7">(Section 2, p. 7)</span>:

$$
\mathbb{E}_t\!\left[r_{t+1}\right] = Z_t\left(\Gamma_\beta f_t + \Gamma_\delta F^{\text{obs}}_t + \Gamma_\alpha\right).
$$

$\Gamma_\beta$ holds the loadings on the hidden factors $f_t$, $\Gamma_\delta$ the loadings on observed factors such as traded benchmarks, and $\Gamma_\alpha$ is the intercept, built from characteristics <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Table 1, p. 7">(Table 1, p. 7)</span>. NA-IPCA, No-Arbitrage IPCA, writes all three blocks' rules in $Q_Z$ and caps how much the intercept may carry. The cap is the "no-arbitrage" in the name: the tighter it is, the closer the model comes to strict no-arbitrage <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 2, p. 8">(Section 2, p. 8)</span>. With the plain ruler and a non-binding intercept cap, NA-IPCA reduces to IPCA <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: p. 22">(p. 22)</span>.

<details class="robustness">
<summary>For specialists: the restrictions, the estimator and the inference</summary>

In $Q_Z$, the latent loadings are orthonormal, $\Gamma_\beta^{\top} Q_Z \Gamma_\beta = I$; the observed and intercept blocks are $Q_Z$-orthogonal to the latent span; and the intercept's size is capped, $\psi(\Gamma_\alpha) = \Gamma_\alpha^{\top} Q_Z \Gamma_\alpha \le \delta$ <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 2, pp. 7–8">(Section 2, pp. 7–8)</span>. NA-IPCA is weighted least squares restricted to this set; its solution is characterised by weighted least-squares equations projected onto the tangent space of the set <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Proposition 3.1, p. 14">(Proposition 3.1, p. 14)</span>. The paper derives rotation-invariant asymptotic inference for the identified spans <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 4, from p. 17">(Section 4, from p. 17)</span>.

</details>

## A simple example {#gf-example}

Take two characteristics, A and B, say two versions of value, that move together across stocks with correlation ρ. The priced direction uses both equally.

An aside: two name tags, "cheap by book value" and "cheap by earnings", keep turning up on the same party guests. The plain ruler reads the tags and counts two traits; the characteristic ruler sees how often they land on the same people and counts the shared part once. Real characteristics rarely duplicate each other exactly (the highest U.S. pairwise correlation is 0.94, <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Table 5, p. 30">Table 5, p. 30</span>), so the shared part is discounted, not merged. And counting traits is not pricing them: overlap describes exposures, not priced risks, a point made in [*Characteristic-Space Metrics*](/research/characteristic-space-metrics.qmd) (p. 32).

::: {.caveat}
**Try this.** (1) Set ρ, the correlation between the two characteristics across stocks, to 0: both splits explain 100% between them. (2) Raise ρ to 0.9: split with the plain ruler, the two blocks claim 190%. **What to notice.** Split with the characteristic ruler, the total always stays at 100%, because block B keeps only what block A leaves unexplained. The shared part is counted once.
:::

::: {#figure-gf-toy .column-body-outset .dfigure .toy role="figure" aria-labelledby="figure-gf-toy-title"}

<div class="figcaption"><strong>How to read it.</strong> Left: the weights that define A and B (gold) and the priced direction (dark). Directions of size 1 lie on the dashed circle under the plain ruler and on the blue ellipse, $a^{\top} Q a = 1$, under the characteristic ruler ($Q$ has 1 on the diagonal and ρ off it). Right: the share of the priced direction each block explains, both rows scored with the characteristic ruler: $(1+\rho)/2$ for A or B alone, $(1-\rho)/2$ for B net of A. The toy's ρ is a correlation between two characteristics, not the weight ρ in the paper's correlation sweep <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Table 10, p. 43">(Table 10, p. 43)</span>, and its percentages are not on the scale of the paper's overlap statistic (0.069 vs 0.0005, <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Table 8, p. 38">Table 8, p. 38</span>). <span class="provenance">Source: illustrative calculation built on the paper's definitions (Section 2; Figure 3, p. 34); no data file.</span></div>
:::

## Design and main results {#gf-results}

The paper estimates the characteristic ruler on the replication panel of @kelly2019characteristics: 37 characteristics including a constant, 12,813 firms, July 1964 to May 2014 <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 6.1, p. 27; Table 2, p. 28">(Section 6.1, p. 27; Table 2, p. 28)</span>. It then simulates 1,000 stocks over 240 months, 300 times, with characteristics drawn to match this ruler, three hidden factors placed by design where characteristics vary most, two deliberately weak observed factors and a nonzero intercept component <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 7.1, pp. 34–36; Table 7, p. 36; footnote 11, p. 40">(Section 7.1, pp. 34–36; Table 7, p. 36)</span>.

::: {#figure-gf-spectrum .column-body-outset .sfigure role="figure" aria-labelledby="figure-gf-spectrum-title"}
<div class="dfigure-title" id="figure-gf-spectrum-title"><strong>Figure 2: The characteristic ruler is strongly uneven.</strong> Share of the total spread carried by each of the first 15 principal directions of $Q_Z$.</div>

![](/assets/img/geometric-framework/eigenvalue-spectrum.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of the share of total characteristic spread carried by each of the first 15 principal directions of the characteristic ruler. The first carries about 25 percent, the second about 15 percent, and every share from the sixth direction on is below 5 percent."}

<div class="figcaption"><strong>How to read it.</strong> Each bar is one principal direction of the characteristic ruler, largest first. Under the plain ruler's assumptions all 37 bars would be equal. <span class="provenance">Source: SSRN preprint, March 2026, Figure 2, p. 33 (reproduced from the paper).</span> <a href="/assets/pdfs/Geometric_Framework_SSRN_7013178.pdf#page=33">Paper page</a></div>
:::

::: {.takeaway}
**What this shows.** The largest direction carries about 25% of the spread and the first five about 62%, against about 1/37, or 3%, each if the 37 characteristics were unrelated and equally spread <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Table 5, p. 30; Section 6.2, p. 28">(Table 5, p. 30)</span>. Size, value, profitability, investment and momentum form tight clusters <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 6.2, p. 28">(Section 6.2, p. 28)</span>. This describes how characteristics overlap, not which directions are priced.
:::

::: {#figure-gf-distance .column-body-outset .sfigure role="figure" aria-labelledby="figure-gf-distance-title"}
<div class="dfigure-title" id="figure-gf-distance-title"><strong>Figure 3: In the headline simulation, NA-IPCA finds the true latent span; IPCA without an intercept block and PCA do not.</strong> Distance between the estimated and the true factor directions (the "span"), geometry-calibrated simulation.</div>

![](/assets/img/geometric-framework/subspace-distance.png){fig-alt="Two bar charts of subspace distance. Hidden-factor directions: IPCA about 0.73, NA-IPCA about 0.01, PCA about 0.99. Observed-factor directions: IPCA about 0.23, NA-IPCA about 1.40, PCA not defined."}

<div class="figcaption"><strong>How to read it.</strong> The distance, $\lVert \sin\Theta \rVert_F$, is 0 for exact recovery and reaches its maximum when the estimated directions are entirely wrong: $\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73$ for the three hidden-factor directions and $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$ for the two observed-factor directions <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: footnote 10, p. 39">(footnote 10, p. 39)</span>. On the observed block the ranking reverses (IPCA 0.23, NA-IPCA 1.40): the design made the observed factors deliberately weak, and NA-IPCA assigns them almost no priced content <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 7.2, p. 37; Figure 4, p. 39">(Section 7.2, p. 37)</span>. <span class="provenance">Source: SSRN preprint, March 2026, Figure 4, p. 39, and Table 8, p. 38 (reproduced from the paper).</span> <a href="/assets/pdfs/Geometric_Framework_SSRN_7013178.pdf#page=39">Paper page</a></div>
:::

::: {.takeaway}
**What this shows.** On the scale from 0 to about 1.73, and with the priced directions placed by design where characteristics vary most, NA-IPCA's hidden-factor directions sit 0.011 from the truth. Those of the IPCA benchmark with no intercept block sit 0.73 away, and PCA's 0.99 <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Table 8, p. 38">(Table 8, p. 38)</span>. The IPCA benchmark also lets its hidden and observed blocks overlap: 0.069 against 0.0005 for NA-IPCA, where 0 means fully separated blocks. The same mechanism as in the toy appears, in a milder form, in a simulated panel of 37 characteristics. This is a comparison, not the effect of the ruler alone: the IPCA benchmark omits the intercept block present in the design <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 7.1, p. 35; Section 7.2, p. 36">(Section 7.2, p. 36)</span>.
:::

<div class="tbl-note column-body-outset">Latent distance: $\lVert \sin\Theta_\beta \rVert_F$ for the hidden-factor directions, 0 to about 1.73. Overlap: hidden–observed block overlap in $Q_Z$. R²: in-sample panel R² of returns. <span class="provenance">Source: SSRN preprint, March 2026, Table 9, p. 42.</span></div>

::: {.takeaway}
**What this shows.** In every row the true directions sit, by design, on the combinations along which characteristics vary most in the U.S. data; only how characteristics are sampled changes <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 7.1, p. 34; Section 7.3, p. 38">(Section 7.3, p. 38)</span>. The IPCA benchmark stays 0.73–0.99 from the truth and NA-IPCA at or below 0.04, even under the identity geometry. The lesson: a good fit is not proof of the right structure. In this design IPCA fits returns with an R² of 0.94–0.99 while missing the true directions, and NA-IPCA recovers them with an R² of 0.58 <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Table 9, p. 42">(Table 9, p. 42)</span>. In the paper's efficiency and stress-test designs, by contrast, IPCA also comes close <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Tables 16–19, pp. 62–64">(Tables 16–19, pp. 62–64)</span>.
:::

## How it relates to prior work {#gf-literature}

The table lists the closest reference points <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 1.2, pp. 3–4">(Section 1.2, pp. 3–4)</span>.

::: {.lit-table .table-scroll}
| Prior work | What it established | What this paper adds |
|---|---|---|
| Approximate factor models [@bai2002determining] | How many common factors a large panel has, under weak dependence | Once the number is set, asks which directions are priced, measured with an estimated ruler |
| IPCA [@kelly2019characteristics] | Characteristics instrument time-varying betas; the model admits an intercept and observed factors and tests whether each is zero | Writes the model's scale and block separation with the characteristic ruler and caps the intercept; IPCA is the special case with the plain ruler and a non-binding cap on the intercept (p. 22) |
| RP-PCA, risk-premium PCA [@lettau2020factors] | Adding a pricing-error penalty to PCA gives factors that also fit average returns | Puts pricing discipline into the set of admissible models, through the ruler and the intercept cap |
| Shrinking the cross-section [@kozak2020shrinking] | A prior that shrinks the stochastic discount factor's coefficients on characteristic portfolios, most strongly along their low-variance principal components | Uses the characteristic ruler not as a penalty but to set the model's scale and keep its blocks apart |
:::

Work on weak and spurious factors [@bryzgalova2015spurious], near-arbitrage bounds [@kozak2018interpreting] and volatility bounds [@hansen1991implications] motivates the simulations' weak observed factors and the intercept cap.

The angle is the ruler. Much prior work first extracts factors with a fixed ruler and then adds pricing restrictions on top <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 1.2, p. 4">(Section 1.2, p. 4)</span>. This paper makes the ruler itself something to estimate. The tools are known; what is new is the ruler as an explicit, estimated object of identification, with an estimator and inference built on it. The evidence supports a specific claim, not a ranking of methods: when characteristics are uneven and overlapping, the ruler changes which directions a model identifies.

This paper first set out the idea that runs through the agenda: take the ruler from the data, and write the model's rules in it. [*Characteristic-Space Metrics*](/research/characteristic-space-metrics.qmd) states the ruler's role precisely: it decides the split, not the fit, and its estimation error belongs in the standard errors. [*Interpreting Pricing Errors*](/research/interpreting-pricing-errors.qmd) holds the ruler fixed to read alphas fairly. [*Characteristic Geometry*](/research/characteristic-geometry.qmd) shows that the ruler's units can move portfolios while forecasts barely move; the [job market paper](/research/characteristic-libraries.qmd) shows that the way the library is written can move holdings with no new information.

## Scope {#gf-scope}

- The paper does not test NA-IPCA on real returns or portfolios. In its simulations, out-of-sample fit is the same for both estimators <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Table 16, p. 62; Table 19, p. 64">(Table 19, p. 64)</span>; a full out-of-sample application in U.S. equities is left to a separate study <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 8, pp. 50–51">(Section 8, pp. 50–51)</span>.
- In the simulations the true priced directions sit, by design, where characteristics vary most, and the IPCA benchmark lacks the intercept block that the simulated returns contain <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 7.1, pp. 34–35; Section 7.2, p. 36">(Sections 7.1–7.2, pp. 34–36)</span>. So the comparison does not isolate the ruler, and it does not show that the characteristic ruler is the right one for real markets.
- The characteristic ruler is estimated from one sample, 1964 to 2014. If the distribution of characteristics shifts, it should be re-estimated <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 8, p. 50">(Section 8, p. 50)</span>.
- The intercept is a capped part of expected returns that the factors leave unexplained. It is not a measured mispricing.
- The large-sample theory holds only under the conditions the paper states; it does not claim that NA-IPCA is the best possible estimator <span class="loc" title="SSRN preprint, March 2026: Section 4, from p. 17">(Section 4, from p. 17)</span>.
